title: July 29th
body:
We arrived in Mendocino just in time to catch the sunset over the ocean after a beautiful drive through the redwoods.

Westy’s newly rebuilt air conditioning was a boon driving through the Sacramento valley! 93-97 degrees outside and we were comfortable!

We camped at Van Damme state beach, cooked a delicious asian-style tofu and veggie starry meal and paid in the morning, earning us a day pass for state parks.

title: July 30th
body:
We woke up to a beautiful view at Van Damme state beach and had coffee in the Westy. Then it was off to Good life bakery in Mendocino for breakfast and gluten-free pastries! As we left, we met a nice couple that gave us Colorado tips and reminisced about their own trips in the Vanagon they used to have. I told the gentleman that I had rebuilt the AC and he gave me an excited fist bump -- these things never have AC!

We wandered around Mendocino, then down to Portuguese beach to swim in the icy cold sea, play with the dogs, and take a piece of driftwood as a souvenir.

Then, we scattered some of Ma’s ashes at the headlands on a little sections of yellow flowers overlooking a cove. I didn’t expect to be emotional, but the tears came, of course. Westy came to take a look and we both sat there with Ma and enjoyed the view for a moment.

We went to a tiny old bookstore and got a used book while Buddy the fat border collie helped us shop.

We were both so happy after our adventures in Mendo, and like the song "Mendocino," we walked through the park, then had to find a little place on School Street that offered a bit of privacy for some afternoon delight.

That night, we headed up Highway 1, and after a quick stop at the beach just north of Ten Mile to walk with the dogs, we camped at a pullout on a cliff overlooking the ocean, where we watched a beautiful sunset while sipping a little of Ma’s favorite wine, Husch Sauvignon blanc. We had a delicious ramen and pad Thai meal with Hodo tofu curry nuggets and slept like rocks.

title: July 31st
body: We drove through the Avenue of the Giants, a beautiful road through redwoods along a creek. We parked the Westfalia near a giant redwood and took some photos, and felt inspired to leave a little of Ma at the base of a redwood that was supporting another, smaller redwood that had been damaged but still grew. We stopped at the Chimney Tree and had a strawberry cheesecake milkshake, which was delicious! We continued on and ended up in Arcata, and on our way to the Arcata community forest, found a group of Westfalias parked in a guy’s driveway! They waved us in, and to our surprise, we noticed there were several “Stephan’s Autohaus” license plate frames — the same one we have! After pointing it out, they said “Stephan is right over there!” We went out to dinner with them at the Mexican restaurant and chatted about race Vanagons, LS swaps, and home made dog food. That night, we slept on Scenic Way at a pullout and fell asleep to the sound of the ocean.

title: August 1st
body: We woke up and made our way to Luffenholtz Beach for some Yoga on the beach with pelicans flying over us! The dogs played with sticks and Miri walked in the surf like a crazy woman and then briefly swam in the ocean. After that, we headed off to Wildflower Cafe in Arcata for delicious gluten free food and iced coffee before a stop at the car show with our new Westfalia friends. We admired many slugbugs, and I was finally able to level the slug bug score - 8 to 8! A Westfalia friend recommended we hike Lady Bird Johnson trail in Redwood National Park, and although dogs are not allowed, she had no issue. We didn’t either, and it was amazing. Beautiful, gigantic redwoods in an almost rainforest-like setting, treetops shrouded in fog, with ferns everywhere and a tree that had beautiful pink flowers on it. We fed Westy almost 2 cans of food before continuing on. After an unsuccessful attempt to view Elk at Elk Meadows, we all (except Miri) were suddenly startled by shrieks of “ELK!!” After pulling over so my heart rate could settle, we saw a herd of 50-70 Elk right next to the side of the road in the yard of what looked like cabins for rent. We watched them graze, flirt, challenge, and do other elk things in wonder, and both Missi and Westy watched intently as they were unsure of what to think about these strange deer-horse-camel things.  We stopped at a Native American-owed gas station where we checked fluid levels, and everything looked great except oil, which was down 0.25qt after 500 miles. We made our way through the Newton B. Drury scenic byway, which was like a much more wild and rainforest-like version of the Avenue of the Giants and offered some amazing views of god rays coming through the redwoods. As it was our last chance to see the coast, we chose to stop for the night in Crescent City where we pulled out onto the pier, admired the sunset (and one another), before enjoying the rest of the Husch Sauvignon Blanc.

title: August 2nd
body: We woke up on the pier in Crescent City, on our 11 month meetaversary, and planned our day — we needed to find water, fill propane, do a little grocery shopping, say goodbye to the coast, and get a SHOWER. Water was found at a community garden, with a hose plenty long enough to reach the Westy parked on the side of the road. Propane at a Chevron, and groceries at ma’s favorite, the used food store (Grocery Outlet). We then set off to say goodbye to the coast, which we did at St George Point, a rock beach full of interesting stones, a sea creature shell (which we took), and dead pelican’s skull, spine, and beak (which we started to take, but the “kelp” we thought was in its mouth was actually skin, so we decided to leave it). We collected a bouquet of wildflowers for Westy’s dash, then headed out! We then stopped by a Mexican takeout joint for a burrito (which took 20 minutes and didn’t come with free chips), and we were on our way. We headed for the Jeddidiah Campground, which has pay showers with 3 quarters and 1 shower token in hand, only to find out that 2 quarters got you a scant 2 minutes and shower tokens were useless! We found a helpful neighbor, Emmie, who had some quarters and hooked us up with $2 worth, buying us a total of 11 minutes of shower, which was just enough and left us feeling amazing. Fresh and clean, we set out on the Redwood Highway and were treated to more beautiful views as we made our way towards Crater lake on the Oregon scenic byway, highway 234. A stop at an Oregon gas station, where self-service is prohibited, almost ruined our trip when the attendant started to grab the diesel pump to fill our van despite us asking for 87! It was quite the shock and we both vehemently corrected the attendant, who was apologetic and offered dog treats to Westy and Missi, who graciously forgave him. We continued on, and a hankering for iced coffee brought us to Patrick Creek Lodge, which was recently purchased by a single mom and two kids with the intent of getting it up and running as a nice forest getaway. The pool may have been murky and green, but the iced coffee hit the spot, and she provided us with a few sugar packets so we could sweeten Miri’s morning coffee. Her 8 year old daughter brought us our change, and we tipped a few bucks before heading on our way. Several slug bug opportunities leveled out the score at 13-13, leaving us tied for the night. We then found our way as close as we could to Crater Lake, setting up camp at a national forest road, but not before preemptively taking the turn and sending the Westy up a nice 45° incline, which she conquered without problem. Hey, there’s the road we were supposed to have taken, and it’s paved! Miri set out for a run with Missi up a forest road that turnbd out to have 1500 feet of elevation gain while Westy and I stayed back, wrote notes, and set up for dinner, sausage and veggies!

title: August 3rd
body: We set out for Crater Lake only to find it shrouded in smoke! The views were still spectacular, however, and we marveled at the beauty from several scenic lookout outs. Miri got some stickers and I got some strategic iced coffee and a chocolate bar (Miri told me to veto her if she ever said no to chocolate, and I took note). More props for the van from random passerby’s — a fella asked if it was OK to take a picture, and another guy congratulated us on keeping it running hehe. We gave the dogs the new chew bones only to discover they’re filled with… powdery meat dust? It ended up all over the floor of the van and Miri nearly died laughing. We drove the scenic Crater Lake loop until the road was closed, then turned around. In order to make sure we go out money’s worth (we paid nothing to enter the park, despite our expired National Parks card, as the ranger station was closed), we decided to steal a tree — a cute little fir looking fella. Miri located the tree, I dug it up, and when we got back to the van, we found that Missi had selected an appropriate pot for it from the trash that she got into — a cottage cheese container! Thus, the tree was christened as “Curd.” Along the way, we celebrated 11 months since our first kiss with many, many more kisses. As we drove through Bend, we discovered why people come to Bend (and why it’s named bend) — to float down the river bends! Miri found us the perfect Thai restaurant — Dear Mom! It had flowers on the sign, tons of flowers in the outdoor seating area, and STRING LIGHTS! We enjoyed our meal, then I did a little shopping at Safeway before we headed out and drove a TON. The wildfire (wildflower) smoke was so bad that we decided to make tracks and find our way to a place where the air would be a little cleaner, which, surprisingly, was a town called Burns. Along the way we saw an abandoned gas station with prices from the early 90s, only $1.26! Sadly, the pumps were not in service. After 2.2 miles of washboard roads, we ended up at a nice little campsite we found on iOverlander, private and at the base of the cliff. After we walked outside we were struck by a beautiful view of the Milky Way! The moonrise took it away, but we both enjoyed it while we could before settling in for the night. The slug bug count stood at 16:14 with Miri solidly in the lead.

title: August 4th
body: Woke up and played ball with the girls before doing a taste test between Folger’s and Starbucks — 2 Folgers were required to get a reasonable taste, so it’s safe to say Starbucks won. Time to escape the smoke of burning Oregon and make our way to Idaho! We saw a huge encampment for fire evacuees  There were wild volcanic lands on our way out of Oregon, and we saw tons of tents at evacuation centers where folks displaced by the fire were taking shelter. Shortly after that, we crossed the time zone line into mountain time, which pushes the sunset back to 9PM, then suddenly, IDAHO! We hit 1000 miles, but somehow missed the 234567 milestone while looking for ethanol-free gas in the suburbs of Boise, which surprisingly look us longer than expected. We calculated around 17 MPG after filling up, so it looks like we’re doing good on gas milage, even with AC! But why is the ethanol-free gas so hard to find? Look out the window, and you’ll see nothing but CORN! After finally finding some ethanol-free gas, we ended up in a little town called Star at a park by the river. The sprinklers on the fresh cut lawn gave us a nice spritz of water and the girls chased sticks out in the river, and I made us quesadillas and cut up avocados and tomatoes to go with Miri’s salad. While driving out, we found Miri’s dream truck, a rust-colored Chevrolet, maybe from the 50s? We took a picture and Miri made me promise I’d find one and LS swap it while she brought me sparkling water and kisses. On the beautiful Banks Lowman road through Idaho, we saw a stunning river and admired it from hundreds of feet above, then we stopped at a gas station that had the oldest pumps I’d ever seen — they counted gas with a rotating dial, and somehow, were ethanol-free. Further into Idaho, we discovered that Miri was right — Idaho is beautiful. Huge mountains, gorgeous rivers, cute cabins, TONS of cows and horses, and amazing scenic views. We ended up at a super cozy campsite near a meadow and small creek off Horse Creek Loop near the Galena Trails. Miri did a little workout in the dust while I wrote this! Slug bug count 19:17, Larry somehow in the lead!

title: August 5th
body: We thought the night would be cold, but I woke up sweating in my thermals and stripped down to my boxers. Phew! We had a beautiful view of the Milky Way and a lovely burbling creek to lull us to sleep. We woke up to a beautiful view of a meadow off Highway 75 at Horse Creek trail and had a slow morning with multiple snoozes, followed by special request tofu scramble and gluten free sourdough toast with cheese. The girls were behaving so good that we were off our guard and I caught Westy in the road and called her back with a scolding. We checked Westy’s oil and found it was almost 1.25qt low, so after a fill up, we were on our way with great oil pressure (39psi at 3000RPM once warm). We rolled into Ketchum and found a super cute coffee shop, Java on 4th, full of wildflowers and cute outdoor seating. We handled Miri’s todo list, got her on my accounts, and filled up Westy’s water with the cafe’s hose. A quick stop at O’Reilly’s got us some extra oil, then continued on past the not-so-impressive Craters Of the Moon national park (where we took a sunflower and a rock before moving on). As the sun was setting, we stopped at the strangely named Beaver Dick park for a quick workaround and played with the dogs, then it was off again. A final a stop at a gas station got us some special Idaho chocolate milk that contains potato flakes! We finally made it to Henry’s Lake, and after trying to make our way to a gated off and rather creepy site we found, we turned around and ended up at a splendid site overlooking the lake and had soup for dinner before falling asleep.

title: August 6th
body: We woke up to a spectacular view of Henry’s Lake, which was more than enough to invite us to go for a swim with the dogs. The water wasn’t too cold, and we swam for a bit while neighbors fished and the girls chased sticks. When we got back to camp, I decided to dry off with a little naked yoga in the sun next to the Westy. I painted Miri’s toenails a beautiful deep blue, then we left with a plan to do the continental divide trail, a little grocery shopping, and a little laundry. The continental divide trail was beautiful and brought us our first taste of Montana, we took in the sights, picked a wildflower, and headed off to do laundry. Unfortunately, the washer laundromat left our “clean” clothes only half soaked and our dried clothes… still half soaked. We hung the sheet and my jeans up to dry and made a note to carry laundry detergent in the future, do smaller loads, and use way more detergent. We headed back to Henry’s Lake to camp for a second night and found neighbors, travelandwork_br, who said they’d be leaving early and didn’t mind us crowding them a bit.

title: August 7th
body:
I woke up early to make sure that mama was able to get her uber to the airport, but I also had Westy maintenance on the mind… The house battery had died overnight and I was wondering why. Sure, we only drove 1hr yesterday, but why was it dead? It turns out the LIFePo4 battery needs over 14V to charge, and the alternator simply doesn’t provide that. I started the van to let the battery charge a tiny bit as I hatched a plan to find a 120V outlet in West Yellowstone and set about making coffee while Miri slept. I let the dogs out and admired the view of the lake when I caught a whiff of oil, so I took a look under the car and found a steady drip of ATF! The red fluid had stained the ground and I was quite alarmed. I knew we had some sort of a leak, but this was heavy! I shut the van off and set about checking the level — it didn’t even register on the dipstick. I added 1.25qt and got it back up to full, but I was worried that we had a serious leak that could result in a catastrophic failure, so I stared calling repair shops to get estimates for a torque converter seal.   After getting estimates of $850-$1000, we decided the plan would be to get a good shower then head out, possibly to Yellowstone, monitoring the level as we went to make sure it didn’t go low. We took a walk down across the little bridge across the creek to the pit toilets with their beautiful murals, I checked out the fish one this time, and we were on our way to a well-deserved shower. Before leaving, we picked up travelandwork_br’s purple dishwashing gloves that had fallen off the hood of their van and messaged them on IG to see if we could give them back… When we arrived, we were blown away to find out that it was $3 for unlimited hot shower time, and we made full use of this magical discovery. I figured now was a great time to put a charge on the LiFePo4 battery with the high speed 20A charger I installed if we could find shore power, and I saw the outlets at a campsite, perfect! But our extension cord was too short. I saw a neighbor with a nice RV across the way and decided to ask if she had one, and she did! She handed me a huge extension cord on a reel and recounted her own struggles being helped by others yesterday when the steering gear on her truck failed, leaving puddles of power steering fluid at the campsite. I plugged the Westy in to charge, turned on the breakers at the campsite after a helpful tip from our neighbor, and set about the longest, most extravagant shower one could hope to have 9 days into a road trip, including a shave and beard trim. I emerged a new man and walked back to the van, hoping to chat with our helpful neighbor. Just about then, she walked over and said “Now you can’t say no, but I’d like you to keep that extension cord.” Of course, I couldn’t say no, so I started giving her a tour of the van and explained we’re on a road trip to scatter ma’s ashes. She confided in me she was in a similar space, grieving the loss of her husband, Roy, who passed away last year and whose birthday was this past Monday. We talked about our losses, therapy, helpful friends, camping, she gave me a tour of her RV (including notes that she had left to her late husband and photos of them camping), I realized her husband was a ham radio operator and her grandpa was a coastguardsman, what a coincidence — my father (and myself and my ma) are ham radio operators and my father and uncle both coastguardsmen! I offered her a cold drink and she countered — “I actually have some food I was going to throw out if you’d like to take it!” I took a few of the items and we kept chatting for a bit, Miri joined us, and we found her childhood dream was to become a ballerina veterinarian, another coincidence! We talked a bit longer as the battery charged, and we offered for her to stay at the dome house some time for free (Miri’s idea) as a token of our appreciation for her generous gift of long-distance energy. She told us of the moose that frequented the campsite area, and shared with us a nice waterfall hike worth going to and we decided that would be our plan for the day. We set out in the Westfalia, excited to see the waterfall, when I noticed there was a bit of a power delivery issue… I pulled over and checked the oil and ATF, no issues, but then I noted a fuel smell coming from the passenger side. After removing the airbox and the MAF, I saw it. A high pressure fuel line feeding one of the injectors was leaking! No worries, I’ll tighten the hose clamp! But that wasn’t it. The hose itself was seeping! On further inspection, the hose cracked and started spurting fuel! This was a catastrophic, no-drive situation. I asked Miri to start calling stores to see if we could get a new injector as the hose seemed to be attached to the injector without a clamp, but we had no luck. A little research later, I realized there was a barb on the injector that the hose slid on to, and all I needed was a 5/16 fuel injection fuel line and I could fix it! I cut the old line off to verify diameter, taking care not to damage the plastic fuel rail, then I started digging, but only found 1/4 line (not for fuel injection systems) and a couple hose clamps. We flagged down a passerby, hoping for a ride offer, and they told us there’s no uber and AAA was our only bet. Miri called AAA, they wanted to tow us and couldn’t help us with our 2.5” of fuel line. I figured I’d hitch hike, but wait, what about Susan, the neighbor at the campsite? I called her and she said she’d be on her way right away. Things were looking up! I went back to stare at the engine bay, wracking my brain for another solution. Could I use fuel line from somewhere else? I only needed 2.5”! Then i remembered something — when I did the coolant reservoir, I saw some hose that was fuel line that really didn’t need to be fuel line, but where was it? I inspected things and found it — the reservoir to overflow line, the one that gets in my way when I check the oil because it’s too long, was 5/16 high pressure fuel injection line! I removed it from the overflow, Miri plugged the overflow so it didn’t drain, I cut it to length, and just about that time Suzan showed up, ready to take me to the auto parts store. I figured hey, I’ll try this solution, and if it doesn’t work, I’ve got a ride. Luckily, it worked. I slid the hose on, connected the injectors, Miri fired her up, and she purred like a kitten — a kitten that doesn’t leak fuel. We chatted with Suzan before she left, and she confided in us that she always wanted children but couldn’t have them, and she found solace in the fact that she could be useful to her nieces and nephews as an aunt. She said she was adding us to her family excel spreadsheet, and as she was pulling away, she shouted “Call me auntie Suzie!” We did the waterfall hike after all — which was spectacular, absolutely striking and definitely more beautiful than Niagara, though I couldn’t appreciate the natural beauty with Miri there, and we annoyed another couple while we giggled and kissed at the prime upper falls viewing spot. We discussed our plans for tomorrow, then headed off to West Yellowstone. We crossed the border to Montana and found a grocery store with — get this — GLUTEN FREE DONUT HOLES! And tofu. And sex towels (which Miri loudly proclaimed mid-aisle). We found our campsite off a forest road, popped up, ate a delicious dinner of butter jasmine rice, veggies, and tofu, and got ready for bed. What a day!

Oh, and it turns out Henry’s Lake has leeches. Good thing we swam in it without knowing!

title: August 8th
body: The idea was to get to Yellowstone before crowds, and we attempted to wake up at 6AM, but a snooze ended up being a stop and I woke up at 7:15AM, an hour late! I put everything away, made coffee, popped us down, took the girls out to hurry, and started driving with Miri still in the bed behind. We had our coffee and donuts on the way, bought a new National Parks pass at the entrance, and our Yellowstone journey began. We took a side road and found a small waterfall, and we were rewarded with an amazing sight — salmon trying to jump up the falls! He tried a few times, unsuccessfully, and we bid him farewell. One of our first stops had bubbling, white paint pits, a geyser that constantly goes off, clear blue springs, and more. We saw the cute old yellow park busses on our way to the next stop, a river fed by a steaming, geothermal waterfall! We check this out, took some photos together, then it was off to Old Faithful. We parked in the shade and left the girls in the car with the fans on and headed to the main attraction. We stood up near the front and heard a lecture by Ranger Steve, who had a well-equipped wheelchair complete with a PA system, radio, and bear spray. He told us facts about how they timed the geyser, how high the water goes, how deep the magma is, and more. As we got closer to launch time, Miri and I scooted up to the very front and sat down criss-cross applesauce for a front row seat. The eruption was beautiful and we cuddled as we watched it. Then it was back to the van for lunch with the girls, who enjoyed tortilla chips. After that, we decided to head to the gift shop to buy some stickers (more on that later), and decided noon was a fine time for ice cream and a coffee. They had gluten-free strawberry cheesecake and huckleberry ice cream, so we got both after the helpful staff double-checked it was celiac safe. We were nearing the time for the second eruption, so we thought we might as well enjoy our ice cream near the geyser while we waited, and this eruption was even bigger than the last! People were very quiet and respectful, except for the kids who bantered about hitting each other and wanting to throw sticks into the geyser. As we were pulling out, we saw a familiar van: travelandwork_br was parked there, the folks who lost their gloves at Henry’s Lake! We gave them their gloves back and chatted briefly, they were very thankful and it was just another case of hilarious serendipity. We headed out again and found more amazing attractions, including dragon’s mouth spring, a crazy cave that spewed steam and belched forth its own waves! We saw roiling gas-fed mud pits, sulphuric caldrons, and then suddenly, BISON! A herd of 109-113 bison, bulls, cows, babies, all wallowing in dust, walking in couples, drinking from the river. We gazed in wonder for a long time (and counted them, Miri getting 113 every time and me getting numbers ranging from 99 to 103). As we continued down the road, we saw a herd of elk, and the whole highway ground to a halt. We watched in wonder, mere feet away. After continuing, we made one last stop — Mammoth Springs because the orange and snow-white ground caught our eyes. The haunting, dead forest among the white minerals were truly impressive, and we made a promise that we’d stop on the way back. As we headed out of the park, Miri squealed “Sheep! Goat! Mountain goat! There!” On the hillside was a mountain goat (or big horn sheep?) pawing the dirt, and Miri somehow spotted him. We stopped in the middle of the road and took in the extremely rare sight of this endangered (?) animal walking around on a more than 45° slope. After a successful search for ethanol free gas, we continued to our campsite — nestled in rocks on a cliff overlooking the valley, made food, and passed out. A long day had filled our eyes with otherworldly wonders and incredible wildlife, not to mention the cranes, swans, and eagles we saw.

title: August 9th
body: We woke up to amazing views of the valley and the beautiful rock formations behind us, cuddled, made love, and had a breakfast — donuts and coffee! Miri finished her gluten free donuts, and to quell her sorrows, we looked up the brand online and found dozens of different varieties, each of which made Miri even more excited to try. Miri did a workout in the dustiest place she could find while I filled out our journal and wrote notes. We ran out of sink water for the first time on the trip, but luckily it was after our dishes were done. We’ll find water today and check out the cute local towns before heading deeper into Montana, towards Bozeman, where a repair shop can do Westy’s torque converter seal, and where I can find an auto parts store to get grease for our clunking CV joint and some extra fuel hose. At the hardware store in Livingston, we saw a Ford truck with a damaged frontend that had a rubber duck stuck in it, and after chatting with the owner for a minute, Miri walked up with Missi in a bucket, we got to talking, and he had adopted two cats from Ukraine! The next thing you know, I’m in his garage doing the CV joint grease and Miri is playing with the dogs in the back yard. Miri went for a walk and met a girl named Jules who is in aviation school in Livingston and has a sponsorship from a South African rhino rescue organization. They went for a coffee downtown and it turns out she needs a veterinarian to come and sedate the rhinos as they get dehorned to prevent poaching — this could be Miri! Otsie and Beth invited us to stay for dinner — homemade chicken curry, rice, and broccolini — and Otsie regaled us with stories of his adventures as a doctor, Vietnam war vet, river guide, pilot, cattle rancher, hunter, and support for tracking grizzly bears. He told us about his wife, an endurance horseback rider and artist who pursued and proposed to HIM, his daughters, a botanist for the national forest and an evolutionary biologist, one of whom is 6’3”, and his son, who passed away at 2 from RSV. We had showers (yay) and ended up staying for the night!

title: August 10th
body: We woke up craving coffee, and boy did Otsie deliver. First, he asked us how we liked our coffee, but before we could answer he was telling another story and ended up making it Otsie’s way — French pressed and made nearly paper white with a generous portion of Bailey’s Irish Cream. This, of course, was a bit outside of our usual routine, and it didn’t quite make us feel awake. We went off for breakfast with Otsie and Beth to a local spot in the Livingston community center that features dozens of his late wife’s original artwork. We didn’t have to order, the food was prepared by the chef based on our loose instructions and though it was delicious, we both felt a little queazy as a result of the runny eggs and ultra-strong spiked coffee. The planned hike and run turned into us just taking a nap in the Westfalia near a beach by the Yellowstone River, and we made plans to head to Bozeman for Westy repair the next day. I worked on notes while Miri slept, and when she woke up, it was time for a dip in the river! A local kid who wore his swim goggles all the way from the parking lot to the water told us of his search for treasure int he river, the dogs chased sticks and had zoomies with an audience who laughed as the girls played, and we sat on the river bed and enjoyed the cold, soothing current. Then, after a craving for burgers, we found Gil’s Goods in Livingston and enjoyed a DOUBLE Beyond burger and a NA beer. A quick stop back at Otsie’s to pick up the print of Elisa’s, and he insisted we keep his bear spray. We did some quick shopping at Albertson’s (and Miri got lost in the gluten free cupcake aisle), then sang along to good music while we drove through the rolling hills and open fields of Montana with the deep red sun setting into the smokey clouds. In the outskirts of Bozeman, we saw dozens of deer, horses, cows, beautiful ranches and homesteads, and of course, one old truck for every man and woman. We made our way up to the campsite, up a dirt road off the Hyalite Creek, and deep into a forested area. When we arrived, we saw two older men packing up a car and they waved us in. We chatted for a bit with Gary and John and confirmed there were no bears, helped them fold up their janky table that fell out of the car when they were backing up, and pulled into the spot for a light snack and some cuddles.

title: August 11th
body: We woke up early at around 7 AM, had some coffee, and got underway to the repair shop in Bozeman, Auto Stop. Taylor had arranged for all the parts we needed, a torque converter seal, axle seals, and a driver’s side axle he was going to harvest the CV joints from. We dropped the Westy off and started walking towards the historic district in downtown Bozeman. We arrived at a coffee shop and l got a latte and a scone while Miri got an iced coffee that turned out to be terrible. There were lots of techy people around and we saw offices for Medium, McIntsh, and Sonos, which makes the vibe quite a bit less quaint. We realized this is the historic brewery district, not the historic downtown, so we started walking that way and found a street with multiple little free libraries, none of which had anything that interesting, but there was a prominently featured DVD of GI Jane that we found kind of funny. We found our way to the historic downtown and saw tons of cute shops, bars, and a natural food store. Our first stop was a dog store where we got a grunting Yeti dog toy, a bunch of treats, and some lamb stomachs (ew!) that Missi picked out. We tried to find a place for me to get a haircut, but everything was booked way out, so we ended up at a bar called IX and the bartender Sophia served us delicious non-alcoholic huckleberry Aperol sprtizes while the girls ate their lamb stomachs, which crunched like potato chips. After that, we found a Brazilian restaurant inside outside in the sun eating our delicious customized bowls — it was Miri's first time having Brazilian food, and she seemed to like it. We walked to the local park behind the library, Miri slept on my chest, then I played with the dogs while Miri slept face first on the grass for a bit. We waited for the call from the shop, and it came at 3PM — unfortunately, we got bad news; the plan to borrow CV joints from the aftermarket axle and swap them onto our stock axle was a no-go, they were different diameters. Taylor told us he had to order a rebuild kit for the stock axles instead and it would be there tomorrow, so we first arranged for them to push the Westy into the parking lot and would sleep on site, but then Otsie texted and asked how the repair was going, and after we told him, he invited us over for another night. Before we left, we sought out the “Espresso and Ice Cream” sign we saw earlier, and ended up having to get espresso and one place and ice cream at another. The barista at the coffee shop asked Miri if the cute guy that came in to check the menu was her boyfriend, so I got that going for me. We combined our espresso with our sprinkle cake and coffee ice creams and enjoyed those with a couple iced coffees, so needless to saw, we were wired. Otsie and Beth were in Bozeman for their monthly pedicures and a Costco run, and they picked us up from Auto Stop, 2 dogs, 3 plastic bags, and one bucket full of weights and yoga mats in tow. We went back to Otsie’s, Miri did a workout and I helped Otsie trim trees that the city said were obstructing the sidewalk and hooked his gutter back up. Westy had a bit of an accident on Otsie’s carpet, it seems the lamb stomach didn't agree with her stomach. Otsie was nice about it and we cleaned it up, so Westy got rice for dinner and a plan to eat only rice and chicken for a few days until it cleared up. I made dinner that evening to say thanks; tofu, stir fry, and lightly fried rice. It was Beth’s first time ever having tofu, and she enjoyed it! Miri had a long shower which set off the smoke detectors, and after that was sorted, we watched The Horse Whisperer, a movie which Miri had never seen, but of course had read the book. It was a great movie but I was TIRED and it took us all the way to 1AM.

title: August 12th
body: We slept in and woke up with a plan to get me a haircut. I knew better this morning, so I made the coffee — sans Bailey’s! Otsie made delicious fruit smoothies, and I made sure to check the protein powder before he put it in, and unfortunately it wasn’t GF, so we skipped it. After that, Miri and I set off to find a haircut, and finally ended up getting an appointment for 1PM. We went back to the house for a bit and chatted with Otsie, then Miri took Missi for a run while I headed off to my haircut at Root 66. The stylist gave me a scissor cut, and we talked about diets, food, running, and of course, the road trip. $25 + $5 tip, 15 minutes later and I was walking back, quite hungry! I stopped at The Pickle Barrel for the 2nd best sandwich in the whole county, the Big Sky — turkey, bacon, and pepperjack. I was hungry so I ordered a whole sandwich, and I was alarmed to find they delivered basically an arm full and probably 3 lbs of sandwich for $29. I ate 1/4 of it and took the rest home for Otsie and Beth, gorging myself on another 1/4 of it. Miri had salad and tofu, I helped Otsie change a lightbulb, Miri cleaned up the dog poop in the backyard, I ordered Otsie a new Aerolatte after finding out his wasn't repairable, and then we looked at pictures of the campsites on the TV for a bit until we got the call from Auto Stop — the Westy would be ready! We asked them to plug it in, packed everything up, and headed out, picking up Beth so she could say bye to us. Otsie let me drive his neat electric pickup truck, and the self-driving features were pretty impressive. We got to the shop, loaded the van back up, and were happy to be on the road again. After a quick stop at Whole Foods and Petco to get Westy a Proviable diarrhea support kit for her digestion issues, we drove back down to Gardiner through high winds and saw a beautiful rainbow over the Montana plains. We camped just up the road from our previous campsite, basically in the middle of an open field with a 360 degree view, and were awarded with a beautiful sunset while we ate soup and quesadillas. The rain pitter pattered on the roof of the Westfalia while the thunder roared softly in the distance as we fell asleep.

title: August 13th
body: We woke up at the gorgeous open campsite above Gardiner and let the dogs run around. I took a hike up above the site and found a juniper tree, and after digging it up, quickly realized it was larger than I thought and wouldn’t fit in another cottage cheese container. Miri had the bright idea of using the empty water jug, so we cut it open and planted it, and she was christened as Crystal, after the Crystal Geyser jug we put her in. Then, it was off for more Yellowstone! We first hit mammoth springs and s saw some amazing mineral formations, then continued down the other part of the loop we hadn’t yet driven. Miri was a bit tired, so she slept in the back while I drove through the rain, then suddenly we saw bison — UP CLOSE! I woke Miri up to see, as we hadn’t yet been this close. They were in a field, grazing and wallowing (though this time, in the mud), with some bulls challenging one another. They decided to move and crossed the road, directly in front of us! The dogs didn’t know what to think, and we moved on. We drove on to Moran and arrived at a campsite near a riverr, late. It was still raining when we pulled up, and we saw tents, towels, and chairs totally soaked by the rain. Miri was craving meatballs, and despite her protests, I had refused to make them for breakfast, saving them for a pasta dinner that evening. She enjoyed her pasta (and meatballs!) with garlic butter, and I opted for the more traditional marinara sauce. We put away a little for tomorrow, both thoroughly sated, and set about cleaning up. A neighbor finally arrived in a hurry and began putting things away. We felt bad for her as it seemed she got caught in a rain storm and hadn’t stowed camp, so Miri and I made hot chocolate and brought it over to the camper, Bev, who is a seasonal worker and has spent the summer traveling and “doing dirtbag shit” with her friends. She was thankful and enjoyed the hot chocolate, returning the cup to us later as we were cleaning up after dinner. We made it an early evening, with me reading my book, American Meteor (finally), while Miri slept. We felt asleep to the calming pitter patter of rain, again. totally covered in

title: August 14th
body:
This morning, we took a long time to get out of camp, for a couple reasons. First, we slept for almost 14 hours, and the residual sleep weighed heavy on our eyelids. That, coupled with the rain made us lazy homebodies, more comfortable cuddling than even going outside to answer nature’s call. Finally, Miri gave me a 40+ minute well-earned massage, further delaying our departure.

Once we finally had camp all packed up, wWe set out to see the Grand Tetons, but Mother Nature had other plans — it was raining and cloudy, so instead of seeing her peaks against a blue sky, we saw them shrouded in fog and mist. A beautiful sight, nonetheless! We paid a visit to the visitor center to buy stickers, of course, and Miri returned a hat she found in the bathroom to lost and found.

We took the Moose-Wilson road through the park hoping to see moose, and despite many signs saying moose crossing ahead, we saw nothing. That said, it was still a beautiful drive and we enjoyed most of it with the window down, despite the showers.

We went onward to Jackson with one major goal in mind — BURGERS! I found a burger joint called Liberty Burger that had a gluten-free bun, sweet potato fries, and an impossible pattyburger! The food was good and we ate it while we watched the rain outside. We sent the poor waitress on a wild goose chase to find coffee, and towards the end of our meal (which was delicious), she arrived with it and it hit the spot for me, but for Miri it only made her want hot chocolate — homemade, in the van. We enjoyed it with several of Auntie Susie’s marshmallows, then set out to walk around Jackson with the dogs. It turns out, those who performed the ritualistic slaughter that was required to make the grotesque antler arches decided that it would be too uncouth to allow dogs within their sordidsolid sanctuary. We still went for a moment, and a sweet young girl petted Missy while her mom remarked “does she have a little poodle in her?” — the one breed Miri is SURE Missy doesn’t have in her. 

We set out for hike at ski resort under the lifts, parking in front of a wedding (or, uh, rodeo) for John & Lisa. We hiked up through rocky switchbacks (on the Uphill Route, which the signs so informatively informed us of), then it was back down through misty trees. We waived at tourists in the lifts and jokingly gave them a hitchhiker’s thumb (and received two in return). After the hike, we walked back to the van and Missy stopped to play with a 3 legged dog, and even Westy was nice to her. As we got to the van, I saw a lady throw her alcoholic beverage can under the car as she was unloading her kids and I gave her a “Oops, you dropped your can!” She didn’t like that much, and said “I’ll pick it up, or maybe you and your old, smelly, ratty dogs can pick it up for me.” After trading a few insults (I called her the wicked witch of the west, she called us smelly hippies, I told her that her plastic surgery looked like shit),. As we went to left, I retrieved the can poured the rest of it on her car. In response, from the depth of her fetid lungs, she hacked up a huge lugey, and like a zombie llama spat on our windshield, twice. About that time, her red faced, short and stout man showed up at her rude beckoning, but told he to leave after she spat on me through my open window, prompting me to say “please don’t spit on me, that’s assault.” We cleaned up, threw her can away, and headed out. I felt bad about inciting her, and Miri didn’t like that I insulted her looks. We talked about it, and in the middle of me sincerely saying I’ll avoid confrontation like that in the future, Miri wore a strange smile… It wasn’t until a few minutes later that she confessed — while I was reassuring her that I would keep her out of situations like that, she had seen 2 blue slug bugs. This brought the score back to a more manageable 28 to 33.

As we continued, we saw a red river off the side of the road and pondered what might have caused it to look that way, when suddenly, we saw it — the confluence of a deep red and pure blue river! We pulled over and walked down to check it out and it was awesome to see the stark line between both rivers as they avoided mixing for hundreds of feet!

We headed out to a campsite near Pinedale — which has all the civilization you need, according to welcome sign — , but the site wasn’t that great, so we drove back through Pinedale to another site, snacked for dinner, and then Miri realized the clouds had parted and gave us a beautiful view of the night sky, including the Milky Way. Prime viewing for the Persieds, which happened to be peaking tonighttoday! We stepped outside to watch them, and instantly saw a beautiful shooting star! We laid on dog beds to watch the show, and though Miri saw a handful more, we didn’t see much as the clouds decided to steal the show. We popped up and fell asleep listeninged to the burble of the creek, and the string lights joined us in popping with a snap and a puff of smoke! It seems whatever wiring issues were causing the flickering had finally snuffed them out….

title: August 15th
body:
We woke up creekside and HUNGRY! We started our day with coffee and gluten-free Basque-style cheesecake, which was exactly what the doctor ordered. Miri did a workout and I fixed the string lights that burnt out with my soldering iron and put our notes back up with double sided sticky tape. The dogs hung out outside and collected a swath of bones from a myriad of different dead animals, no doubt deposited there by a predator of sorts. We were hungry, and it wasn’t quite breakfast time anymore, so we made burgers, and despite this being the second meal in the row that we had burgers at her insistence, Miri still insists it’s not her favorite food.

We made a plan to drive to Mirror Lake and camp for the night and set out. Then it finally happened, we saw moose! Miri spied it while driving, and instead of screaming “LOOK!” or something of the sort, she very calmly said “There’s your moose!” as she pulled around to park. It  was aA baby and his or her mom, down a hill near a bridge, in a field of purple and yellow wildflowers! We parked and walked to see them,  and I cried a little as the baby moose watched us back — it’s like it was me and ma! They were magnificent, larger than I imagined, and I scattered a little of ma’s ashes, telling her and told her that I hope she enjoys the moose watching.g before we moved on.

As we were pulling in for some ethanol free Dino juice, we saw a sign “Wild horse viewing area” — so naturally we banged a u-turn and drove out. Sure enough, there were dozens of wild horses that had been corralled by BLM, and you can own one for around $185! Miri picked out several and we talked about all the horses she wants, the rusty red truck, and the rusty red horse trailer. I got a neck massage during this, which prompted me to let her know we could stay as long as she wanted.

We planned the rest of the trip, stopped to check the oil (0.75qt low), and torque of the CV joints (all slightly loose, but not too bad). Miri checked out a point of historical interest, which, for probably the 4th time in the trip, told us that we were sitting on the continental divide.

We bumped some funky old music and sang along, and I learned Miri had never heard “Tutti fruiti” as she was snacking on a jelly bean by the same name (not from the seat, this time). I taste tested each of them to ensure she wasn’t surprised by a buttered popcorn or cinnamon bean, and I felt quite useful.

As we drove through the Wyoming plains, we saw tons of antelope by the side of the road, against a backdrop of yellow and green plains, mountains, and clouds.

We stopped for gas, we calculated our gas mileage again at 18.3mpg, and with the 7-10% correction for our incorrect speedometer, that’s over 20mpg! Nice one, Westy! We met some folks at the gas station that knew where Pollock Pines was, which was mighty surprising, and we watched a beautiful sunset as we headed towards our campsite.

And our campsite was HIGH. We started climbing, staring out at an already impressive 7000 feet, and made our way higher and higher as the sun sank low… 8000ft… 8500ft… 9500ft! Miri finally guessed right after 4 guesses, but we kept going up! Finally, as we hit 10000 feet, the turn came for our campsite. The site we had planned for was taken, so we continued down the very rough road until we found a sort of camped on spot that seemed just right and pulled off.

I made us green curry ramen, tofu, and veggies, while Miri fed the dogs (including the “bad” local cottage cheese she refused to eat for like a week) then we enjoyed some chocolate and cocorolls and wrote this journal entry.

Again, the night sky didn’t disappoint. The Milky Way was on full display, then as I stepped out, I was greeted by a beautiful shooting star.

Just before bed, we heard a little rustling outside of the van, which surprisingly didn’t cause the dogs to alert, but set us on edge. A wild animal? We had a group peeing activity and quickly realized there were two pairs of eyes watching us. They were a far distance away and I wasn’t scared, but Miri was alarmed by a strange sound, which fortunately (or unfortunately) turned out to be me passing gas. We laughed and turned in for the night, with a full appreciation of how comfortable we can be around one another, and how safe it feels to have someone who loves and cares about you by your side while you pee (armed with a bright flashlight and bear spray, of course).

title: August 16th
body:
I woke up early to nature’s call and found the field we parked in by a burbling creek shrouded in a low lying mist as the sun rose behind the trees. The road wasn’t as crazy as it felt driving in, and we saw a Subaru and a truck pulling a trailer passing through. Iowa license plates. Still dressed in their Iggy suits, the Dino dogs sunned themselves on the rocks while we broke down camp. Today’s goal was to conquer the Medicine Bow Peak and lakes trail, a 7+ mile trail with 1,800ft of elevation gain. We pulled into a lot and saw… men and women absolutely dressed to the nines — suits, dresses, makeup, and perfect hair? At a trailhead? It was a wedding! We congratulated the bride and groom — a beautiful, svelte black woman and an unremarkably average white guy (with a cute sense of humor) — as we laced up our boots.

We started the hike and it went from a simple trail to some pretty rocky scrambling. The views kept getting better and more expansive as we went, 3 miles into it to the final climb to the Medicine Bow peak. We zoomed up the last section and found a nice place to sit with the dogs, took a bunch of photos of the incredible view, and ate pretty much all the food we brought with us, except for a protein milkshake that ended up being just a companion we brought on the hike just so we could drink it, lukewarm, thereafter.

We continued down the trail, with me lamenting the downhill rock scramble while Westy was quite unsure of where her next foothold should be, requiring much urging to jump between rocks. As the trail leveled out, we met a beautiful couple, Blake and Molly, who live locally in Laramie. Blake is a photographer and spoke with a Tennessee twang, Molly is a professor. Their dog, Gia, was a huge black labradoodle, and they also dabble in van life in their Sprinter Revel. They shared tips on places to go from here to Utah, restaurants in Laramie, and more. We invited them to come stay with us in Pollock Pines if they’re ever in town, exchanged numbers, and continued the hike.

I know we’re in the Rocky Mountains, but WOW. The rocks were amazing. Red, green, marbled, crystal, I could hardly take my eyes off the trail to look up at the amazing view of dozens of lakes because there were so many neat rocks. The bag got heavier and heavier the further we went as we couldn’t stop adding rocks to our collection.

Those boots we laced up, it turned out, ended up being the bane of my existence. I’d never done a hike this long with them, and I realized they’re too small, causing pain in my left foot. Miri and I switched shoes, and I immediately twisted my ankle. I vented my frustration as we sat on a rock, collected myself, apologized for being dramatic, and we continued. Walking past mirror lake, with a beautiful view of the mountain we had just conquered, wildflowers, and, well, a mirror-like lake. Miri did her magic and took some adorable photos of Westy and Missi, but not before they galavanted through the field and into said mirror-like lake. 

We finished the hike up and my feet were hurting pretty fierce, so Miri told me to go dip them in the ice cold lake while she loaded the dogs up. The water was so cold my feet became numb, and I had to take them out and put them in the sun. Just about then, I saw the Westfalia going up the road, park, and Miri jump out with my sandals. She came tromping through the creek, oblivious to the fact that she was splashing through where fisherman and photographers were busy practicing their craft, delivered my sandals to me, and we walked back together, with my arm around her, borrowing a little support from her shoulder.

We were HUNGRY, and we almost popped up at a lookout to cook sausages, but a craving for Thai food had us plotting a route to Laramie. We stopped at a cute queer coffee shop/bookstore called Nightheron, got some delicious iced coffees, then went to Agong Thai next door and put in our order. I asked the gal behind the counter if she knew where a hose was, and a helpful gentleman answered — just stop by the Territorial Prison… Don’t worry, it’s no longer a prison, it’s a museum now! After a grocery stop, we hit the prison and, sure enough, there was a hose there. We filled up on water (verrrryyyy slowwwwlllyy) while Miri organized the van and put away groceries. After a quick stop at Big D’s oil for some ethanol free Dino juice, we were on our way again, a long boring drive through Boulder and Denver at night convinced us we missed nothing, and we parked at a pullout just above the paint mines, unaware that we were about to be transported to another world.

title: August 17th
body:
We woke up with crime on our minds. Well, not right way, first I cleaned up a bunch of trash from previous visitors, then grabbed my shovel. Miri helped me pick out a nice 3-headed cactus, which stabbed the shit out of me as I dug it up and planted it in a cottage cheese container. Cactus Catie was now on board!
 We made our way to the paint mines, used their pit toilet, and then set off — dogs in tow — to explore the mines. Almost immediately, we met a trail ambassador who asked us how our day was going before informing us that dogs weren’t allowed as they would damage the fragile ecosystem. We took them back to the van, popped up, set up an array of fans and a water bowl, and set out to explore.

The paint mines were breathtaking. Despite the small size of the park itself, it was super impressive. We felt like we were explorers on another planet full of crazy colorful spires and hills formed of some hitherto unknown alien minerals. Pinks, yellows, oranges, and blinding whites. Crystals, clay, red rocks. Otherworldly and magical. As I am but I man, I had to touch, and I found the clay walls had some give to them! So naturally, the next logical thing to do was lick, so we both did. The rocks did not taste like snozzberries, but they did have an interesting texture. I found some very interesting rocks and some clay, which we grabbed, and I cleaned up a bunch of random pieces of trash as my penance for the crime of attempting to bring mutts in to the paint mines.

We came back and found the van cooler than the outside, threw our trash out, and continued on our way, plotting our route to the Great Sand dunes. We needed fuel for the drive, so we made a stop in Pueblo. We walked into the 3 Birds coffee shop and were immediately pegged as being Californian. Miri asked why, and the lady said “Because you’re tall, hot, good looking, and beautiful.” We got gluten free macrons, caramel cake, and bread pudding, and Miri scarfed down the caramel cake and took a bite of the bread pudding. Unfortunately, about an hour later, Miri realized she had been mildly gluten’d, probably by the bread pudding, and that necessitated a quick stop at a gas station to evacuate all stomach contents.

We arrived at the Great Sand Dunes at around 6:45PM, just in time! We had about an hour to hike to the top to enjoy the sunset over the dunes. The hike starts with a walk across an expansive sand desert. The ground absorbs extra energy with each step as your shoes fill with sand, but it’s only a taste of what you’re about to experience. As the climb begins, you realize what it must be like to trudge through the desert. Each step is labored, requiring way more than the usual amount of energy as you slip in the sand beneath your feet. We saw folks boarding down it, families walking together, and we let the dogs run free — after tethering them together. They ran their hearts out as ours pounded out of our chests, the steep ascents unrelenting. As we began to crest the largest dune, the beauty came into focus. Why is this here? A desert, in the middle of the mountains, a gorgeous sunset with godrays coming through the mountains and clouds. We plopped down in the sand, after a dog photo shoot, of course, and I chatted with our neighbor. He called out “Come on mom, you’re almost here!” I shared with him the purpose of our trip, and he remarked that the memories he’s making with his mom on their trip will last forever. They will indeed, and how lucky we are to have a chance to make them; him with his mom in her mortal form, and us, with ma, in her spiritual, infinite form, guiding us to beauty, new friends, happy coincidences, love, and a life worth living to the fullest.

We drank wine, ate potato chips by the fistfull to replenish the energy we burned climbing the dunes, and let the wind cover us in sand as we cuddled and watched the sunset. We ran down the dunes together, hand in hand, laughing and full of energy from the beauty we took in (and the wine). Missi led us across the desert directly to the van, I toweled the dogs off, beat the sand out of our shoes, and we loaded up, heading for a campsite above the park. We turned up the tunes and sang along, happily honking the Westy’s horn.

We arrived at the Zapata falls trailhead, had burgers, and turned in for the night.

title: August 18th
body:
We woke up with one phrase on our collective mind: “All right,” which was said to everything. It was a slow morning for me, and it took some time for me to properly wake up, no doubt due in part to the wine enjoyed at the dunes and the grueling hike up. We had coffee and drove up the road to start the Zapata falls hike, which was really only a half mile there and a half mile back. After a half mile, the creek starts and you have to walk through it to the waterfall, which comes out of a rock wall and cascades down into the creek, absolutely beautiful.

However, walking through the creek seems to catch many hikers off guard, and they end up with soaked shoes and leave their wet socks to dry, forgotten, and destined to become part of the ever so aptly named Zapata Trail — which means shoe in Spanish. I guess they just wanted to leave their socks in a fitting final resting place — a shoe.

We continued on and hunger forced my hand, causing us to make a stop in the town of Del Norte. I spied a natural food store called Simple Foods with a little shaded area out back, so I walked in to check, and yep, they had gluten free sandwich options! We ate our sandwiches with some cheese curls and a lady took a picture of Missy — she looked like a mini version of her friend’s dog.

We continued through Hermosa, where we stopped to let the dogs hurry and check the oil — 0.6qt low after around 800 miles. We had a little more than 1/4 tank of gas, so I stopped at a gas station which had a sticker that said “Contains trace amounts of ethanol” in red and another black sticker that said “Contains 10% ethanol.” Miri and I took that to mean that the 91, with its red label, was ethanol free, but everything else was 10%. The gas station attendants and owner had no clue, and he tried to tell me that octane rating was the percentage of gas to ethanol before googling and finding out he really had no idea. We threw 1.986 gallons in for good measure and headed up the crazy steep pass, Wolf Creek, after which we were rewarded with some amazing views. I told Miri stories about my grandma, and she learned ma’s middle name is Ann, remarking that “Sharyl Ann sounds like a cute doll’s name,” which made me smile.

After that, we entered the tiny town of Silverton, an old Colorado mining town. We decided not to stop and began our drive on the Million Dollar highway, and wow, I can see why it’s named as such. In the first 30 seconds, we had to u-turn to photograph an amazing red mountainside reflected in a pond, right on the side of the road. We continued and saw breathtaking views, crazy sections of switchbacks, old mining operations that were being restored, and some nice birch trees… So naturally, we got out and I started digging one up, but the rocky ground they like to grow in refused to yield, and I think I damaged its roots. We planted it anyway and flooded its soil, hoping it figures things out.
 
After a couple stops on the Million Dollar Highway to admire the view and look for big horn mountain sheep and Canada Lynx (we saw none), we continued into Ouray, which is apparently the Switzerland of America. We figured it would be easy to find laundry and a shower, but when we rolled into the RV park that had the laundromat, we found out it was member’s only! About that time, an older couple walked by and started talking to us about the van, with the gentleman remarking that he had a pink Chevy panel van in the 70s with flowers all over it. I told them we were looking to do laundry, and they were kind enough to share the laundry code (0346), some detergent, and even a handful of quarters! Margie and Mike then let us plug in to their hookups to charge the LiFePo battery and urged us to use the same code to take showers (was it that bad?). We put the laundry in and both enjoyed showers, though Miri’s was less enjoyable as she got temporarily locked out of the shower room and then the lights went off every 5 minutes and she had to exit the shower stall and wave her hands to get them back on. While she was busy with that song and dance, I folded and put away all the laundry and got us ready to depart.

We picked out a couple locations and tried our luck, but all the forest roads were closed, one with a proper road closure blockade, and another with… a handwritten sign held up with paracoad and a blue carabiner… We turned around anyway, heading back through Ouray and up the Million Dollar Highway to another potential spot, which unfortunately was a tiny bit up the 4x4 only Alpine Loop… Its tiny gatekeeper was too much for the Westy, even if the basic gravel road that followed was doable, so we turned around. It’s about midnight at this point, but we’ve got some promising options even further back up the Million Dollar Highway, so we headed back up the mountain pass, finally arriving at Ironton Staging area, made the bed with fresh sheets, fed the dogs, and had a little soup before crashing at around 1AM, our latest bedtime yet!

title: August 19th
body:
I woke up at our campsite in the forest, popped up and made coffee while Miri slept. After morning coffee and the GF macarons, we chatted for a bit, talking about how Margie and Mike had driven all the way across the US from Florida to San Diego, almost the longest way you could do it — almost. Driving from Virginia to California, with a few stops at National Parks along the way, is a bit longer. Miri reflected on this, how she ended up in a gravel lot in Pollock Pines wondering what she was doing, cursing herself for not taking the job offers she had in Hawaii, Montana, or even Truckee. Why Cameron Park? She didn’t really know it then, but it was probably Ma’s meddling, sending her to a really less-than-desirable place so she could end up almost getting ran over by me, fall in love, and end up on this road trip with me. A constant source of happiness, adventure, excitement. Gratitude, affection, intimacy, and respect. Everything I need in a woman, and what a good woman I found it in. You really do find the best things on the side of the road.

The dogs sat outside and Missi buried her bone for hard times, nudging the dirt and patting it down with her nose in the cutest way imaginable. Westy politely asked for a little water, I set our plants out to get some sun, then cleaned the van up a little. Miri went for a workout while I heated up my breakfast, a guilty pleasure, Jimi Dean sausage egg and cheese croissant. Bob Marley played in the background, prompted by our talk of the fact that Miri could have been in Hawaii right now instead of Pollock Pines.

Drove Million Dollar Highway again, stole a birch tree but probably killed it.

Got wine for neighbors, but they were already gone.

We got beet burgers, annoying gay shop owner, drew us on the wall, met another celiac. grumpy brewery

Looked at South Rim of the Black Canyon of the Gunnison

Drove to Bob and Eileen’s and arrive a little bit too late they already ate. Had a nice dinner, corn, rice, soup, and shared System Update beer with Bob and Eileen. Talked for hours, caught up.

Plugged in the Westy and went to sleep. Westy dog woke me up several times to go out.

title: August 20th
body:
We woke up and had Eileen’s homemade granola and yogurt, plus some local Palisade’s peaches. We decided we’d all head out to the North Rim of the Black Canyon of the Gunnison, Bob and Eileen included, and check out the dog friendly viewpoints and the Chasm Trail. 
Eileen picked up a trail guide and we started the Chasm Trail, learning along the way about PJ forests and pegmatite granite. Bob pointed out the cobble river rocks at the top of the canyon where the river ran billions of years ago and explained that, 1 stop before the trail guide told us the same. Being a little ahead of the textbook is the sign intelligence, I think. Curiously, we learned the canyon was carved by water, not seismic activity. This blew my mind, because how could this happen? Apparently, a large deluge could cause as much riverbed carving as 50 years of normal activity, and Bob recalled a story where, in 1999, he watched a river in Yosemite flood and carve feet of riverbed out. Miri and I both found it amazing that he could recall this exact event, the date, and vivid details. A reminder to make those vivid memories that stick for decades, indeed.

We said our goodbyes at one of the viewpoints, and I thanked Bob and Eileen for the involvement they’ve had in my life, from the early mentorship in computer science, to the help with my car hobby, to the psychological support when my mom passed. With Bob’s tip that there was an ethanol free gas station in Hotchkiss, we headed that way. We knew we’d end up with very little gas in the tank, but it seemed like we’d arrive no problem based on the GPS. After we took a turn, Bob texted to ask if everything was OK because they didn’t see us behind them, and luckily, it was. We stopped for a Burrito and iced coffee in Hotchkiss, and after a detour trying to find the station and ending up at a closed petroleum company in a tiny town, we got 13 gallons of ethanol free gas at a tiny gas station. We got some ultra-expensive El Dorado water at another gas station, dropping off the gallon we filled from Bob’s due to its strange smell, and the kind old attendant (with her LED name badge that read Trish, I think), granted us permission to use their hose to fill up our water tank.

Further down the road, we saw a neat bus with imagine world peace on it, pulled in, and let the girls hurry — their tummies still aren’t right, so it’s, uh, not great, but it’s better than littering.

We stopped in Grand Junction for an extended and much needed resupply. Safeway for food and drink, Petco for more Proviable for the dogs, and Home Depot for a Dewalt USB-C charger so we could keep the fan blowing — we’re heading into the desert and need as much airflow as we can muster!

We headed down the road and made the call to camp halfway, just across the Utah border at BLM lands, Wetlands, about 1 hr from Arches. An open field, open hearts, open minds.

title: August 21st
body:
We woke up a little late again and had coffee and blueberry gluten free pie for breakfast! Quite the treat, but not quite enough to keep us fueled for the day. 

We took Highway 128, at the Wyoming Gal’s recommendation, and it didn’t disappoint. Why isn’t THIS a national park? We saw big horn sheep by the side of the road, did a double take, and u-turned to see them again. Ferraris and Porsches raced down the road along the Colorado river. We stopped for frozen coffee pops and ended up with free water and ice.

After a stop for more ethanol-free gas, we ended up at a little restaurant in Moab, Gloria’s, and I got a turkey bacon wrap. Miri got a rainbow bowl with tofu, and our server, Cass, was… taller than her?!
On the walk back to the van, we met some folks of unknown descent that really liked the van, gave them a quick tour at the sidewalk. They’re driving all the way from New York to see a few national parks and then heading all the way back!
We started our journey at Arches, but of course the first stop had to be the visitor center for some stickers! Once that was handled, we headed out with a plan to see a few spots on the way up and a few on the way down. Park Avenue looked amazing, and we made our way past Balancing Rock, the 3 Gossips, Sheep Rock, and up to Windows. Everything was breathtaking, but then the Westy took our breath away with the smell of fuel… I got under the van and heard some rough sounds from the fuel pump and then boiling gas in the tank! It was under a deep vacuum when I removed the gas cap, which isn’t a good sign. I decided to remove the o-ring from the gas cap, but we started losing power — the van barely moved unless we were going downhill. We decided to end the arches exploration and coasted back into town. Destination: O’Reilly’s, our favorite store! It turns out there’s a CarQuest right next door, and though O’Reilly’s came up short, CarQuest had a pump that worked from a specifications perspective, except for the 3/8th inlet and outlet — we needed 1/2 inlet and 5/16th outlet! After a quick stop at the plumbing store minutes before it closed, I had the adapter I needed for the inlet and was able to swap the pump out in the O’Reilly’s parking lot while Miri did a little yoga and walked the dogs.
With the Westy finally getting the fuel it needed, she was so much quicker! After a test drive and another look at the pump under the car to confirm all was well, we decided we’d head out but make it an early night. We continued on our way, heading towards the Corona Arch hike when we saw the hills change color — they looked reflective. Small raindrops began hitting our windshield, and I said “we’re about to drive into a wall of rain!” And we did. Beautiful, warm rain, blue skies on one side, thunder and lightning on the other. We rolled down the windows, stuck our hands out, and laughed out loud.
We rolled into the campground across from the trailhead, grabbed a pay slip, and pulled into spot #3. We watched a bit of the sunset and thunder/lightning show, but Miri was famished so I got dinner going — sausages, veggies, and pasta. We ate at the picnic bench (our first one on the whole trip) until the bugs had other ideas and we had to come inside.

title: August 22nd
body:
We woke up early, by our standards, at 7:40AM. I made coffee and woke Miri up with coffee and a gluten free muffin, and we ended up sharing two. I had my yogurt, we threw some water and an Oiko in the backpack, and we were off to do the Corona Arch hike! We popped down and drove across the street to the trailhead and hopped out with the pups. Beautiful red rocks, red dirt, and an amazing views of two spectacular, gigantic arches. We met a fella from London and took photos for him, and he returned the favor. The girls scrambled like pros, and a couple with a cattle dog that was stuck whining and jumping into their arms were super impressed with Missi. Once we got to the second arch, The Pinto Arch, we decided a lone tree in the arch was a perfect place for ma to watch the sunset, lightning, and observe the beautiful red rocks, so we left a little of her there. Westy walked up and sat down, then as we gathered our items, lingered around next to ma. It was an emotional moment, but we were quickly laughing again, enjoying one another’s company, making jokes about Missi’s service in the Ukrainian army, and taking in the beauty outside.

We decided we wanted another stab at Arches National Park, and it did not disappoint. This time, the weather was a little nicer too — overcast and slightly lower temps! The arches were beautiful, and the Fiery Furnaces were super interesting. We nicknamed one of them Penis Point and were surprised it wasn’t on the map. We did the walk to the Delicate Arch viewpoint, but after doing Corona Arch in the morning, it was wholly underwhelming, despite its freestanding status. The drive back was equally breathtaking, and Miri took over so I could see the sights.

After considering other local activities, we decided heading for Great Basin and covering as much Utah ground as possible was the right move. Miri decided it was a great time for a nap, and I drove between ethanol free gas stations until she woke up and we decided to call it early and pull into a dispersed camping site near Dmad reservoir. I calculated our gas milage, first at a paltry 16.4MPG with mountain passes, and then a striking 19.7MPG on flat ground (on Highway 50, nonetheless!). We pulled into camp after passing the Bull of Dmad, who, presumably, is the animal the reservoir is named after, because he looked mad! Once at camp, Miri decided it was prime time for a workout, so I joiuned her for a bit, then took a bird bath with baby wipes. Miri came for her headphones, and said the mosquitos were biting her, so I got the mosquito spray and noticed the disco light we had failed to use the entire trip so far! I pulled it out, remembering it has a bluetooth speaker (which I had just been lamenting the fact we didn’t have one, using the stereo pulls lots of current from the already low charge LiFePo house battery). I connected to it, but there was no sound. Oh! The wires were disconnected internally, I remember this! I dug for my tools and pulled out the soldering iron, repaired the wires, and hooked it up to the new Dewalt USB battery pack, and damn, we were jamming! Just then I walked outside and saw how cool the canvas looked, so I grabbed Miri’s phone to take a video and caught the lightning in the background!

I settled back to do some journaling, fixed, the notes on the wall, and get ready for a dinner — fake chicken fried rice!

title: August 23rd
body:
We woke up by Dmad reservoir with showers on the mind. Miri found us a perfect little setup at an RV park across from the visitor center for Great Basin, and we decided we’d hit it after checking out a hike to a natural arch — the only dog friendly hike in the whole park. We plotted a course and ended up on a rough road with ruts that would require Jeep-like articulation. Instead of trying our luck, we tucked our collective tail and headed back with a plan to ask at the visitor center what the best course of action was. We arrived at the visitor center, and Miri had an important question. She pulled no punches as she asked it: “Why is this a national park?” Apparently, there are some really old pine trees, and in order to protect them, it couldn’t just be a national forest. But that’s about it.

We started up the scenic drive at Great Basin, a 3000ft climb to 10000ft. I’ll admit there were some decent mountain views, but the view of the valley, far outside of the park, dappled with mile wide patches of shade, was the most impressive part. We made it to the end of the scenic drive, only to have a little trouble starting Westy and some strange noises from the fuel pump. Maybe it’s the 2 gallons of E10 we put in? Who cares, it’s downhill from here and it’s time for a long overdue shower!

We arrived at the RV park, asked if we could plug in to charge (yes!), and decided the best course of action was for us to take the dogs with us into the shower/bathroom so they wouldn’t get hot. The shower hit the spot, I got a shave in too, then I waited for Miri outside in the heat. 5 minutes or so and my hair was dry, just in time for a bald fella to walk up and chat us up about the van. He traveled for work, and so did his significant other. They spent 3 days here, and one of the highlights was swimming in an almost empty lake and seeing some deer. Neat. I’m not sure we’ll be back.

A bit down the road, I lamented the fact that we didn’t have a bench seat, and I invited Miri to cuddle up. We both needed that closeness, and the void between us — a mere 18 inches — seemed like the black canyon. We both scooted closer and she cuddled up to me. We kissed. One thing led to another, and we’re flying up a road that was more a rock crawl than a drive. We pull off, draw the curtains, and I dive face first into her. We cleaned up and drove back down the road, totally satisfied. Totally happy. What more do you need? Love, the open road, a shitton of dogs, a fridge full of goodies, a couple gallons of water. One another.

Onward, to a tiny town called Ely, where I spied some good gas and some gluten-free pizza! She ordered the veggie, and I got the Miner Special, which had all the good stuff — pepperoni, bacon, mushrooms, bell peppers, onions. A total dream. We ate half with a NA beer and a kombucha from the car, then stored the rest. After a quick stop at a very much closed feed store, we continued to the local grocery store. The folks were strange, the selection was decent though. We got everything we need and plotted a course to our camp spot for the night — a lunar crater! Why is it a lunar crater? Apparently, astronauts used to train here. Regardless, it’s the most interesting thing in the entire state of Nevada, and we can camp by it because it’s BLM land, so let’s send it.

Highway 50 is apparently the most lonely highway in the country, but Highway 6 gives it a run for its money with a sign that says “No services for 167 miles.” We did some quick calculations and found… There’s no way to get ethanol free gas on our path to Mammoth, and even once we’re back in CA, we’re SOL. But do we really need it? We kept seeking it out, with the intention of protecting our oft-broken van, but now there was no way. Maybe we were babying her all along and she’d be fine? After all, Cali gas is all E10 anyway… We decided to sally forth, across the endless valley, past the only sign of life — oil refineries, and their companion, those creepy oil derricks that see-saw back and forth, sucking raw Dino juice from the earth. There’s something unsettling about them.

We drove into a beautiful sunset, not the colors, but the clouds that somehow traced the mountains, their strange shapes imitating their earthbound brethren. We put on some good music for a bit, but then shut it off and just enjoyed each other. Miri got us to the campsite, 7 miles down washboard roads at almost 60MPH for most of it, right on the edge of the crater.

Tonight, we camp on the moon, next to a crater. Stepping out, moon rocks crunch underfoot. There’s no life here, save for some alien plants (and the pervasive sage brush that occupies every square foot of BLM land). Craters of the moon has nothing on this.

title: August 24th
body:
Gluten free donuts and a 2nd cup with a view of the crater, huge and impressive! Tons of lava rock scattered around the site, of course, including the fine gravel that crunched underfoot.

I felt like doing a little yoga, but it was quite sunny crater-side. I deployed the awning for the first time on the entire trip, put on Pink Floyd’s “Dark side of the moon” and started stretching.
